tasks.short: Operate telephone, intercom, radio and announcement equipment, and report communication faults.

steps.what: Check telephone console status, queues and available extensions.
Use console controls to connect, hold or reconnect calls.
Contact colleagues through intercom or radio and relay operational instructions.
Make routine announcements using public-address equipment.
Describe equipment faults and send them to technical support.

tasks.design: Configure queue controls and exception alerts in the {TELEPHONY}; routine connections follow approved destinations and fallback rules. Use approved announcement templates in the public-address category of {OTHER}, with operator approval before broadcast, and a structured fault form in the {WORKFLOW} that creates a ticket in the {HELPDESK}. Intercom and radio conversations stay human, supported by the current contact directory.
tasks.previous_blocker: Equipment controls, directories and fault reporting were separate. Radio exchanges and physical controls offered little useful integration.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing call controls cover routine connections. AI-assisted coding can reduce the effort of building fault forms and connectors; no autonomous agent is needed.
tasks.still_hard: Older radio and public-address equipment may lack supported interfaces. Live coordination, outages and unusual announcements still need an operator.
tasks.human_edge: The operator understands local context and can coordinate clearly when normal communication channels fail.
tasks.altitude: The week contains fewer console actions and repeated fault descriptions, with more attention available for live coordination. No new decision rights are assumed.

reach.task: Triage communication equipment faults before escalation.
reach.learn: Read basic console diagnostics, identify affected users and collect reproducible fault details.

evidence.claim: Teams Phone Agent can route calls; this supports configuring routine telephone connections.
Structured fault forms and template announcements need deterministic controls, not a model.
In the Netherlands, operator monitoring or recording may require works council consent under WOR article 27.

assumptions: Time shares and remaining percentages are planning estimates, not measured savings.
The telephone share uses console screens and phone controls; the prior's in-person share is too broad for equipment operation.
Intercom, radio and public-address equipment are categories of {OTHER}.
This task covers equipment operation; caller intake is described separately and savings must not be counted twice.
Build ranges cover a limited pilot with supported interfaces. Consultation follows applicable national rules.
unknowns: Which communication equipment and supported interfaces are installed?
Which announcement templates and destinations are approved?
Who can authorize broadcasts and connection-rule changes?
What employee consultation and access approvals apply?
What proportion of console actions already happens automatically?
research_questions: Can the installed {TELEPHONY} handle holds, retries and fallback destinations through configuration?
Does the public-address equipment support reviewed template playback?
Which diagnostic fields can populate a fault report without collecting unnecessary personal data?
new_work: Review queue and equipment exceptions.
Maintain destinations and approved announcement templates.
Check failed ticket creation and connector errors.
Test fallback operation after equipment or configuration changes.

tasks.short: Greet callers, understand requests, provide basic information, transfer calls and record messages.

steps.what: Answer the incoming call and greet the caller.
Ask whom the caller needs and what the call concerns.

loop.input: Caller speech and an approved list of routine request categories.
loop.output: Request category, requested name and an uncertainty flag.
loop.check: Validate allowed categories; resolve names against the directory; never accept invented destinations.
loop.stop: At most two clarification turns or 45 seconds; uncertainty, urgency or a human request transfers immediately.
loop.why_not_simpler: Callers describe routine requests in varied speech. A fixed menu remains an available alternative.

steps.what: Clarify difficult requests and support upset or vulnerable callers.
Find the requested person, department or alternate contact in the directory.
Consult reference information and answer a basic caller question.

loop.input: Caller question and retrieved, approved public reference passages.
loop.output: A short answer with its supporting passage identifier.
loop.check: Require a current approved source and supported facts; exclude personal records and discretionary advice.
loop.stop: One answer attempt and one clarification within 30 seconds; unsupported questions pass to an operator.
loop.why_not_simpler: A fixed answer handles exact FAQs. A bounded loop handles varied wording across approved reference passages.

steps.what: Transfer the call and explain the fallback if the recipient is unavailable.
Take callback details and send the message to the recipient.

loop.input: Caller message speech and fixed callback fields.
loop.output: Draft recipient, caller name, callback number and short message.
loop.check: Validate required fields and number format; read details back; operator approves before notification.
loop.stop: One extraction and one correction; unresolved details go to manual message taking.
loop.why_not_simpler: Names and message content arrive as free speech. Fixed fields and deterministic checks bound the extraction.

tasks.design: Configure greetings, directory lookup, transfers and fallback queues in the {TELEPHONY}, with directory updates from the {HCM}. Add bounded speech intake and an answer desk over approved {DOCS}; disclose AI interaction, meet applicable synthetic-audio marking requirements, and pass urgent or uncertain calls to a person. A message form in the {WORKFLOW} timestamps drafts and notifies recipients after operator approval, including next-shift review of non-urgent out-of-hours messages.
tasks.previous_blocker: Directory lookup and routing were already configurable, but varied speech and message content needed manual interpretation. Reference information was often scattered or stale.
tasks.enabler_now: Voice intake, approved-source answers and directory disambiguation are available today. Small connectors and validation rules can now be built with less development effort.
tasks.still_hard: Noise, names, accents, distressed callers and stale contact data cause failures. Message-taking evidence is limited, and fluent answers can still be wrong.
tasks.human_edge: A person can recognize confusion, build trust and interpret a caller's needs beyond an approved FAQ.

ambition.what: Non-urgent callers seeking callback intake outside staffed reception hours.

tasks.altitude: The week shifts toward difficult calls, reviewed messages and fixing recurring information gaps. No new authority over customer commitments or urgent-call decisions is assumed.

reach.task: Prepare a callback case that the next team can resolve without repeated intake.
reach.learn: Capture the minimum useful context, verify contact details and distinguish information from a customer commitment.

reach.task: Turn a caller message into a clear written callback brief.
reach.learn: Check factual wording, preserve uncertainty and avoid adding promises.

evidence.claim: Teams Phone Agent answers approved questions and routes calls, including in Dutch.
Teams Dial by Name supports partial names and disambiguation; directory changes can lag by up to 24 hours.
Webex AI Receptionist answers from uploaded files and transfers calls; Dutch is absent from the cited locale table.
An unnamed academic hospital reportedly automated about 13,000 weekly calls with about 50% lower central reception workload; the vendor case states no method.
The AI Act requires disclosure of AI interaction and applicable machine-readable marking of synthetic audio.
A bounded message extraction and readback workflow is plausible, but the digest provides no documented message-taking case.
The cited tribunal case held the organization responsible for incorrect chatbot advice.

assumptions: Steps describe common branches of call handling; one call need not pass through every branch.
Time shares and remaining percentages are estimates. Machine steps move exception effort into human handling and new work.
Telephone conversation is represented as paper_phone; the prior's large in-person share does not describe face-to-face work here.
Routine answers are limited to approved public information. No agent is required.
GDPR applies to caller data. Retention, access and the lawful basis must be established before using recordings or transcripts.
National employee consultation rules may apply. The pilot estimates include access and consultation work, but elapsed approval time may be longer.
This task shares routing components with equipment operation; implementation costs and savings must be deduplicated.
unknowns: Which languages, call types and volumes occur?
Which reference answers are approved and who maintains them?
How current is the directory, and which fields may callers hear?
Which urgent-call destinations have reliable human coverage?
What lawful basis, retention period and recording notices apply?
Can staff review messages during calls and after an out-of-hours intake period?
Which installed features and licenses already cover the proposed functions?
research_questions: How accurately does bounded intake resolve real names and requests across representative audio conditions?
Does directory disambiguation expose information beyond approved public contact details?
Can answer validation reject unsupported advice reliably?
What caller abandonment and operator handoff rates occur in a limited pilot?
Can callback details be read back accurately without retaining full call audio?
new_work: Review message drafts and unresolved callback details.
Handle human requests, uncertain answers and failed transfers.
Maintain approved answers, directory mappings and fallback destinations.
Review sampled call outcomes without inferring employee emotions.
Maintain retention controls, disclosure wording and connector health.
Check the out-of-hours message queue at the next staffed shift.

tasks.short: Welcome visitors, confirm hosts, register visits, issue badges and arrange escorts.

steps.what: Welcome the visitor and ask whom they are visiting.
Match visitor details to the expected visit in the visitor-management system.
Notify the host that their visitor has arrived.
Confirm the visit and agree who will escort the visitor.
Enter visitor details and arrival time in the visitor-management system.
Check permitted access, assign a security badge and hand it to the visitor.
Introduce the visitor to the escort and explain site instructions.
Collect the visitor badge when the visitor leaves.
Record departure and close the visit in the visitor-management system.

tasks.design: Configure the visitor-management category of {OTHER} to reuse expected visits, timestamp arrivals and departures, and notify hosts through the {CHAT}. Host approval precedes admission, and the receptionist confirms badge access before issuance; supported badge-return events close the visit automatically. A connector to the {CALENDAR} can remove repeated entry while greetings, badge handover and escort introductions stay human.
tasks.previous_blocker: Host confirmation, visitor records and badge controls were separate. Physical reception and access decisions cannot be replaced by a data-entry shortcut.
tasks.enabler_now: Structured forms, host approvals and event-based updates are established technology. AI-assisted coding makes small connectors easier to build; a model is unnecessary.
tasks.still_hard: Walk-ins, unavailable hosts, identity mismatches and restricted areas require local judgment. Physical badges and access-control interfaces vary.
tasks.human_edge: The receptionist welcomes people, notices situational problems and challenges access requests that do not fit the visit.
tasks.altitude: The week has less rekeying and fewer host-chasing messages, leaving more attention for arrivals and exceptions. Admission and badge decision rights remain with the authorized people.

reach.role: first-line supervisor of office and administrative support workers
reach.task: Plan reception cover around expected visitor arrivals.
reach.learn: Interpret arrival patterns, estimate physical handover time and protect visitor privacy in staffing reports.

evidence.claim: Visitor registration, notifications and approval records can use deterministic forms and workflows.
Physical badge handover and context-sensitive admission decisions retain substantial human work.
The supplied digest contains no visitor-management product or documented visitor-management case.

assumptions: The baseline uses an existing visitor-management system; paper visitor books remain possible customer variants.
The visitor-management and badge access-control categories use {OTHER}.
Shares describe the end-to-end visit, including host effort; operator-only estimates should exclude host time.
Remaining percentages are estimates and retain physical handover effort.
Badge return can generate a supported departure event; otherwise a person must confirm checkout.
GDPR applies to visitor records. Access and retention must follow the established purpose.
Access changes and any employee monitoring require review under applicable national rules.
unknowns: Is visitor registration handled in a system, on paper or through another means?
Can expected visits and hosts be read from the {CALENDAR}?
Which people may approve visits and badge permissions?
Can badge assignment, return and deactivation produce supported events?
What identification checks and escort requirements apply?
What retention and consultation requirements govern visitor and host records?
research_questions: Can existing configuration provide host approval and notifications without custom code?
Can visit and badge events be linked without exposing unrelated calendar information?
What fallback works when the visitor system, host notification or badge equipment fails?
new_work: Resolve unmatched visitors and unanswered host notifications.
Review missing checkouts and unreturned badges.
Maintain host mappings, access templates and retention settings.
Test badge deactivation and outage procedures.
Correct duplicate visits and failed calendar synchronization.

tasks.short: Monitor alarms, handle emergency calls, route assistance and broadcast approved emergency announcements.

steps.what: Watch the alarm panel and acknowledge incoming alarm signals.
Check the alarm location and circumstances against the emergency procedure.
Answer an emergency call and establish the caller's location and immediate need.
Choose the response destination and escalation under the emergency procedure.
Connect the emergency call or contact the designated response team.
Broadcast the required emergency announcement over the public-address system.
Copy alarm times, routing actions and announcement times into the incident log.

tasks.design: Configure alerts in the alarm-system category of {OTHER} and present the relevant approved procedure from the {DOCS}; the operator interprets emergencies and chooses the response. The {TELEPHONY} executes an operator-confirmed destination, while deterministic templates in the {WORKFLOW} prepare announcements for approval and broadcast through the public-address category of {OTHER}. Supported event logs feed an incident chronology through the {DATA_PLATFORM}, removing manual copying while retaining manual fallback controls.
tasks.previous_blocker: Alarm, telephone and announcement equipment had separate controls and logs. Reliable emergency integration required commissioning and failure testing, not better language generation.
tasks.enabler_now: Supported event interfaces and deterministic templates can remove navigation and copying. AI-assisted coding reduces development effort, but does not remove the need for emergency testing.
tasks.still_hard: Ambiguous locations, simultaneous incidents, failed connections and equipment outages need trained judgment. Physical systems and response procedures are expensive to test properly.
tasks.human_edge: The operator interprets incomplete information, stays with a distressed caller and coordinates the response under pressure.
tasks.altitude: Emergency work contains less searching, dialing and copying, with more attention available for callers and response coordination. No new emergency classification or dispatch rights are assumed.

reach.role: first-line supervisor of office and administrative support workers
reach.task: Organize reception emergency drills and review communication failures.
reach.learn: Use incident timelines, test fallback channels and distinguish a control failure from a training gap.

evidence.claim: The AI Act lists AI emergency-call evaluation, classification and dispatch-priority setting as high-risk uses.
Teams PSTN usage reports contain call times, numbers and durations; they support telephone chronology, not alarm or broadcast logging.
Operator-confirmed destinations and fixed announcement templates can use deterministic controls.
The AI Act prohibits workplace emotion inference except for its stated medical or safety exceptions; this design uses no emotion inference.
In the Netherlands, operator monitoring and recording can require works council consent under WOR article 27.

assumptions: Alarm handling and emergency-call intake are alternative entry branches, not mandatory sequential actions.
The prior's large in-person share represents live communication; actual work combines alarm screens, procedures and telephone equipment.
The alarm and public-address categories use {OTHER}.
Only repeated chronology copying is eliminated. Incident interpretation and narrative reporting remain human.
No model evaluates emergency severity or assigns dispatch priority.
Action gates use the authorized operator's immediate confirmation within existing procedures, without a separate approval queue.
Time shares and remaining percentages are estimates; drills must verify whether the proposed controls help.
GDPR applies to incident and caller records, including any health details. Employee consultation follows applicable national rules.
Build ranges assume supported interfaces and a limited site pilot; equipment replacement would require a separate estimate.
unknowns: Which emergency procedures and response destinations are approved?
Who is authorized to acknowledge alarms, select destinations and broadcast announcements?
Do alarm and public-address systems expose reliable event logs and control interfaces?
What independent controls remain available during outages?
Which incident records contain health or other sensitive personal data?
What commissioning, drill, access and employee consultation requirements apply?
research_questions: Can existing controls provide one-action connection to an operator-selected destination?
Can templates validate location and broadcast zone without interpreting emergency severity?
How does the workflow behave when contacts are unavailable or multiple alarms arrive?
Can event logs produce an accurate chronology across clock differences and missing events?
Which failure tests must pass before the controls enter operational use?
new_work: Maintain emergency contacts, location mappings and approved announcement templates.
Run drills and test independent fallback controls.
Review missing events and incorrect incident timestamps.
Add human incident narratives and response outcomes where needed.
Verify connection success and investigate failed broadcasts.
Review access, retention and employee monitoring settings after changes.

role.altitude: The role shifts from repeated connection controls and record entry toward difficult callers, visitor handling and emergency coordination. Existing authority remains in place; any broader staffing or service decisions require explicit delegation.
reach: Customer service representatives: prepare useful callback cases and resolve simple information gaps.
Computer user support specialists: triage communication faults using structured diagnostics.
First-line supervisors of office and administrative support workers: use arrival patterns and incident reviews to improve cover and drills.
skills_to_grow: Check directory matches, message drafts and approved-source answers.
Handle distressed callers and uncertain requests.
Use diagnostic information and write clear fault reports.
Understand visitor access, personal-data minimization and retention.
Test communication fallbacks and maintain emergency readiness.
role.ambitious_version: Provide non-urgent callback intake outside staffed hours, with next-shift human review, while using saved reception time for complex callers and physical arrivals. Shared directories, routing controls and event logs form a reusable starting point; emergency interpretation stays with trained people.
